doc.title: Wilson "Chembo" Corniel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, November 15, 2019

title: Why clave matters and how it frames phrasing
summary: Clave is a two-bar phrase that organizes writing and phrasing; the instruments imply it even when it is not played.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: to the music. They say, “La clave es la llave.” The clave is the key. Okay? So the reason why is that when you play clave, which is say a three-two, I’m going to tap it like [claps] right? Everybody knows that. This is a two bar phrase. One-two-three-four, one-two- three-four, one-two-three-four, two-two-three four. Right on two-three-four, two. So this is a two bar phrase. In that music we write in two bar phrases so you won’t jump. In jazz you do one bar, one bar here and there, and that’s why you know you might do a two-bar phrase generally but if you put in an extra bar here and there it flips it around. So this is why it’s so important like when you’re writing a Latin tune, that is the basis first of all, that it’s even. You’re writing every two bars.
Why would you choose to do the two-three clave as opposed to —

Well it depends on the phrasing, on the phrasing that you want to do. Like say you have a phrasing in your mind with the horn [scats] two-three, it’s a pick-up. You know? So it depends on the phrasing and then that’ll show you what side of the clave to put it, and then you start there and you continue. Now the reason why we phrase around that clave as a frame, because that’s what the dancers dance to.
But someone — it doesn’t always have to be played. Is that correct?

No. It’s not being played but it’s emphasized on each part of the instrument. It’s accented on the three, you hear a certain downbeat, you hear a certain phrase [scats]. He’s phrasing I allowed it, so he’s telling me where the clave is. There’s a bass pattern [scats] — so now I know where it is on the bass so by his phrasing. So this is after years of, you have to have it engrained you know, but first you’ve got to figure it out and follow it. When I play a tunbao on the congas I’m playing, I’m hitting a certain part of the clave too so my rhythm is also telling everyone where the clave is too, in the way I phrase it: two-three- three-two, the accent’s where I’m going to hit the and of four or on the fourth beat [scats]. So when you hear that downbeat on the four you know it’s three sides, the fourth meet on the third side, see? So it’s all in the instruments. So once you get used to it, and then when everybody’s phrasing on it, you can’t lose it. You know? You hear it.

Yeah I know, but I’m talking about for us who know this is how we get into that. So but the timbale player will hit a rhythm on the side, like he was showing the drummer. [taps] So if the drummer is on a cymbal [scats]. So he’s playing that phrase, so he’s playing with the clave too. So you go [scats] you see? So therefore this is what we try to do and what we did yesterday with me, Cascadu and Victor with the percussion, all those rhythms from all around the world that we try to — it’s so much more than what we did. But we got to learn it from the folkloric from the really root of each rhythm, from where they come from.
